title: Problem Set 1 Formatting Requirements
markdown:
## What this covers

This chapter is not a lecture but a piece of course infrastructure: the "Formatting requirements"
note attached to Problem Set 1 in Stat 243 (Statistical Computing, UC Berkeley), read across the
four semesters the department's repositories preserve — Fall 2021, Fall 2024, Fall 2025, and Fall
2026 — together with the problems that note was attached to. It assumes only that the reader is
about to submit a problem set in a course like this one and wants to know what a submission is
actually required to look like, and what has stayed fixed while the course's toolchain changed
underneath it. There is no mathematics to derive here; the content is a submission contract, and
the value of reading all four versions together is seeing which parts of that contract are
policy (constant across tool changes) and which parts are just consequences of whichever language
and platform that year's PS1 happens to use.

## The submission contract that holds across every year

Every version of PS1's formatting note reduces to the same handful of requirements, independent of
whether the target language is R, Python, or bash:

- **One dynamic document, not a document plus pasted output.** The solution is a single file that
  mixes prose and code chunks — an R Markdown or LaTeX+knitr file in 2021 (`ps1.Rmd` / `ps1.Rtex`),
  a Quarto file in every later year (`ps1.qmd`). Longer functions can live in a separate code file
  and be pulled into the document (via `inspect.getsource()` in the Python years), but the document
  itself is what gets rendered and graded.
- **The submitted PDF must be the one the document itself produces.** All four years say this in
  almost the same words: the PDF handed in is the PDF that comes out of rendering the qmd/Rmd, not
  a document assembled by hand. The 2024/2025 notes make the reason explicit — the grading rubric
  expects output to appear *because* the code chunk ran during rendering, and rules out
  copy-pasted output or screenshots entirely.
- **Text is part of the answer, not a wrapper around the code.** Every version asks for prose
  describing the approach and the steps taken, separate from whatever the code itself shows.
- **Code needs comments**, in particular at any line or construct that would not be obvious to
  someone else reading it — not a comment on every line, but coverage of the non-obvious parts.
- **Show enough output to demonstrate the code works, not all of it.** A short example run is the
  target; dumping everything the code could produce is explicitly discouraged in every year.
- **Collaboration is allowed, but has to be disclosed.** 2021 and 2024 state this directly: name
  anyone you worked with (or say you worked alone), and note in text or code comments any specific
  idea or code taken from another student or an outside source — 2024 even names ChatGPT as an
  example of a source to credit. 2025 and 2026's problem-set text doesn't repeat this paragraph,
  but both still point back to the syllabus policy on working together, so the underlying
  expectation has not visibly changed — only the reminder was trimmed from the PS1 boilerplate.
- **The GitHub submission is named and organized according to a separate submission how-to**,
  linked from every year's note but not reproduced by it. None of the four sources here spell out
  those naming conventions; they live in `howtos/submitPS.html` (or the 2021-era
  `howtos/submitting-electronically.txt`), outside what was converted for this chapter.

## What changes from year to year, and why

The visible differences track the course's toolchain, not a change in what counts as a good
submission:

| Year | Document format | Code language in PS1 | PDF submission channel | New in this year |
|------|-----------------|----------------------|-------------------------|-------------------|
| Fall 2021 | R Markdown / Rtex (knitr) | R | Gradescope | — |
| Fall 2024 | Quarto (`ps1.qmd`) | Python | Gradescope | linting (Problem 3); environment/requirements file (Problem 4d) |
| Fall 2025 | Quarto (`ps1.qmd`) | Python | Gradescope | same as 2024; module file requirement made explicit in the submission list |
| Fall 2026 | Quarto (`ps1.qmd`) | bash | **Pensive** | notes on bash-chunk quirks (below); `sed` flagged as likely sufficient, `awk` optional |

Two changes are worth pulling out on their own.

**The submission platform for the rendered PDF moves from Gradescope to something the 2026 note
calls "Pensive."** The source gives no further explanation of what changed or why — it is simply
named as where the PDF now goes, alongside the unchanged expectation that the qmd and PDF are also
committed to GitHub.

**The language taught in PS1 moves from R (2021) to Python (2024, 2025) to bash (2026)**, and the
2026 note explains this is because that year's PS1 draws on Units 1 and 2 rather than Units 2 and 4
— an unrelated reordering of the syllabus that happens to change which unit's tools this problem
set exercises first.

## A shell-specific gotcha: bash chunks don't share state

The 2026 note flags something the earlier, Python-based years never had to warn about: **variables
set in one bash code chunk are not visible in the next bash chunk**, unlike Python chunks in the
same Quarto document, where state persists across chunks in the usual way. Each bash chunk in a
Quarto document runs as its own subprocess, so anything assigned with `x=...` in one chunk is gone
by the time the next chunk starts.

The note's advice is procedural rather than technical: test the mechanism itself, early, with a
disposable qmd file containing a dummy bash chunk, well before the due date — "we're quite happy to
help in advance; we're not happy to help the night before the PS is due." If a script needs a value
computed earlier, it has to be recomputed, written to a file and read back, or otherwise passed
explicitly between chunks — it cannot simply be assumed to survive the way it would in R or Python.

## Reproducibility additions from 2024 onward

Starting in Fall 2024, two requirements appear that are absent from the 2021 note:

- **Lint your code.** The formatting note points at Unit 4's section on code syntax and style and
  asks that it be applied to the webscraping/API problem (Problem 4 in 2024 and 2025), using a
  tool such as `ruff`. Both years note the same practical wrinkle: linting is straightforward for
  code kept in a separate `.py` file, but there is no clean way offered to lint code sitting
  directly inside a Quarto code chunk — the 2025 note is explicit that this is unsolved ("I don't
  know how to lint code in a qmd file") and invites students to post a fix if they find one.
- **Include an environment file.** Problem 4d in both 2024 and 2025 asks for a requirements file
  (pip- or Conda-based) recording the Python package versions the code was run against, checked
  into the GitHub submission alongside the qmd, the module file, and the PDF. This is the same
  reproducibility idea Unit 4 covers more generally, applied here to make one specific submission
  reproducible.

Neither the 2021 (R) nor the 2026 (bash) note asks for an equivalent environment-capture step —
the requirement is specific to the Python years, tied to the package-manager tooling Python has and
bash, as taught here, does not.

## Exercises

These are the actual PS1 problems from each of the four semesters, reproduced from the formatting
note's companion "Problems" page. They are not solved here. Read the surrounding formatting
requirements above before attempting any of them — in particular, whichever year you are working
from, remember what document format, language, and submission channel that year's contract asks
for.

### Fall 2026 (bash / shell)

1. Read the linked lecture notes on computer architecture (CMU's *Statistical Computing*
   materials) and briefly describe the difference between disk and memory. Note, in your own
   words, what kind of data-analysis situation would run out of disk space versus run out of
   memory.
2. A friend is planning a wedding in Death Valley National Park in March and wants it as late in
   the month as possible without a high chance of a very hot day. Using data from the Global
   Historical Climatology Network, and doing all of the work in bash except part (c):
   a. Download yearly climate data for a small, deliberately limited set of years into a temporary
      directory, reporting to `stdout` the number of observations found for each year (including
      zero), while suppressing incidental output such as download progress. All steps must be
      shell commands saved in the solution file, not a description of manual downloading.
   b. Subset the combined data to the Death Valley station, the `TMAX` variable, and March, writing
      the result to a single file. The station ID must be obtained programmatically from
      `ghcnd-stations.txt`, not hard-coded.
   c. Write a short Python (or R) script, called from the shell, that reads the file from (b) and
      produces a single plot of side-by-side boxplots of maximum daily temperature for each
      calendar day in March.
   d. Generalize (a) and (b) into a shell function taking a location string (not a station ID), a
      weather variable, and a year/month range as arguments, returning the results without the
      per-year row counts. The function should validate its arguments (including an ambiguous
      location string), print help for `get_weather -h`, and clean up any raw downloaded files.

### Fall 2025 (Python / GitHub API)

1. As in 2026, describe the disk-versus-memory distinction from the same reference, including when
   a data analysis might exhaust one or the other.
2. Using the ideas from Unit 2, Sections 1–3, on reading and writing data and on plain-text versus
   binary file sizes (numbers generally taking 8 bytes each in binary):
   a. Generate a `numpy` array `x` (20 columns, standard normal entries) with enough rows to reach
      about 16 MB, showing the arithmetic used to pick the row count.
   b. Explain the sizes of a CSV and a pickle file written from the same (rounded) array, including
      an estimate — from first principles, not `wc` — of the CSV's character count, and whether
      rounding to four decimal places would have made the CSV smaller than the pickle file.
   c. Writing the same numbers one per row (no commas to save) leaves the file size essentially
      unchanged — explain why.
   d. Compare the speed of `pandas.read_csv` against `pandas.read_pickle` on the same data.
   e. Time reading the first 10,000 rows of the CSV using `nrows`.
   f. Using `skiprows`, test whether reading an equal-sized chunk from the middle of the file is as
      fast as reading the same-sized chunk from the start, and say what that implies about whether
      pandas has to pass over the intervening rows.
3. Read Unit 4's section on code syntax and style, apply it to your Problem 4 solution, and lint
   your code (e.g. with `ruff`). Briefly note what you changed as a result, and flag anything in
   the reading you'd have done differently.
4. Using the GitHub REST "commits" API on the `numpy/numpy` repository:
   a. Write a function that issues the GET requests needed to retrieve commits (up to the API's
      100-result cap) and returns them as a Pandas or Polars dataframe with a reasonable set of
      fields; it should work on any public repository.
   b. Plot a histogram of commits per user, clearly labelled.
   c. Write a function that finds the most prolific committer, fetches that user's GitHub profile,
      and returns it — printing a short summary unless a verbosity argument turns that off.
   d. Package (a)–(c) into an importable module usable on any repository.
   e. Include a pip- or Conda-based requirements file capturing the environment used.
   f. *(Extra credit.)* Retrieve thousands of commits rather than the first 100, and plot how
      commit volume varies over time.

### Fall 2024 (Python / webscraping)

1. Same disk-versus-memory reading and short comparison as above.
2. The same file-size and chunked-reading problem as the 2025 version (parts a–f), unchanged in
   substance.
3. The same code-style-and-linting reflection tied to Problem 4, unchanged in substance.
4. Webscraping Google Scholar for publication data (Google Scholar has no API):
   a. Search Google Scholar for a researcher of interest (Michael Jordan is offered as the
      reference case) and, from the "User profile" result, extract the HTML element containing
      their Google Scholar ID.
   b. Write a function that builds and submits the HTTP GET request for a given ID and returns the
      resulting HTML. If Google returns "429" errors, fall back to `curl` (directly or via
      `subprocess.run`), and avoid re-downloading while developing part (c).
   c. Write a function that parses that HTML into a dataframe with title, authors, journal,
      year, and citation count as columns, and test it on a second researcher.
   d. Include a pip- or Conda-based requirements file capturing the environment used.
   e. *(Extra credit.)* Write a function that extracts the Google Scholar ID itself from a
      downloaded search-results page, without ever querying Google Scholar via `requests`.
   f. *(Extra credit.)* Extend the scraper to retrieve all of a researcher's results, not only the
      first 20.
5. Inspect Google Scholar's `robots.txt` alongside Unit 2's discussion of webscraping ethics, and
   say whether scraping Google Scholar this way looks permissible — and why Problem 4 stopped short
   of automating the ID lookup in part (a).

### Fall 2021 (R / webscraping)

1. Read the "Memory hierarchy" and "Cache in depth" sections of the linked piece on CPU cache,
   RAM, and disk (no submission required for this part).
2. Using Unit 2, Sections 2–3, on reading data from disk "online," in chunks:
   a. Generate a CSV of random real-valued numbers, 10 columns, sized to about 100 MB, showing the
      arithmetic used to size it.
   b. Time reading the first 100,000 rows with `read.csv()` or `read.table()`, repeating the timing
      and checking whether `colClasses` speeds it up.
   c. Using `skip` and `nrows`, test whether a middle chunk reads as fast as a same-sized chunk
      from the start, and say what that implies about whether R passes over the intervening rows.
   d. Read the same data sequentially in equal chunks via a connection, and check whether reading
      the middle chunk this way costs the same as in part (c).
   e. Save the matrix with `save(..., compress = FALSE)` to a `.Rda` file and explain its size
      relative to the CSV.
   f. Repeat with a matrix of one repeated value and `compress = TRUE` (the default); compare the
      compressed sizes of the random and constant matrices and say what that suggests about
      compression.
3. Read Unit 4 (Sections 1.2–1.3) on good programming and project practice, apply it to Problem 4,
   note briefly what you changed as a result, and flag anything you'd have done differently.
4. Webscraping song lyrics from MLDb:
   a. Using `read_html()`, work out how to search MLDb programmatically by title and "all words,"
      handling both the case of a direct lyrics page and a results table (compare "Dance in the
      Dark" against "Leaving Las Vegas"). Also say what the `si` query parameter controls. Insert a
      short `Sys.sleep()` between repeated queries to avoid triggering "503" errors, and develop
      the HTML-parsing code against a downloaded copy rather than re-querying repeatedly.
   b. Write a modular R function that, given a title and artist, finds the exact matching song on
      the first page of results and returns its lyrics, artist, and album(s) — or `NULL` if there
      is no exact match. (`stringr`'s `str_detect`, `str_extract`, `str_split`, and `str_replace`
      are suggested as enough string handling; regular expressions are not required.)
   c. Extend the function to handle both the direct-hit and multiple-results cases gracefully,
      including invalid input or no result from MLDb.
   d. *(Extra credit.)* Handle searches that return more than one page of results.
5. Compare MLDb's and Google Scholar's `robots.txt` files against Unit 2's webscraping-ethics
   discussion, and say whether scraping each one this way looks acceptable.
6. This problem is the formatting of the submission itself: (a) format the document according to
   the requirements above (nothing to submit for this part); (b) *(extra credit)* demonstrate the
   `reticulate` package's ability to pass data between R and Python chunks within one R Markdown
   document, with some processing done on the Python side.

  page, the Global Historical Climatology Network, the GitHub REST API docs, Google Scholar, and
  MLDb) that are named here but not reproduced, exactly as the source notes leave them.

  (`howtos/submitPS.html`, or `howtos/submitting-electronically.txt` in 2021) and grading rubric,
  neither of which was supplied as an input to this chapter and so is named but not summarized.
